#Databases

A database server on one of your machines, brought up by serviceman in docker, always up, its data kept there. An app picks one of its databases in its Data tab and finds it in DATABASE_URL at every start, as a user of its own; an Adminer given one opens on it, logged in.

The page is Databases in the rail: each server, its machine and how it stands, and a row per database in it, with its tables, its size and the apps that picked it.

#A server

+ MySQL and + PostgreSQL ask four things:

  • Machine: one that is online, with docker its agent reaches; the others are listed, greyed, saying why.
  • Version: MySQL 8.4 or 8.0, PostgreSQL 17 or 16, the official image, docker.io/library/mysql:<version> or docker.io/library/postgres:<version>.
  • Filled with: nothing, or a sample (below).
  • Name: mysql-1 or postgresql-1, the first number free; up to 40 small letters, digits and hyphens.

Bring it up, and the server says each step as it takes it: pulling the image, making its container, waiting for the server to answer, fetching the sample, loading it. Then it is up, its databases listed. A step that fails leaves it failed, with the reason; its + with the same name on the same machine brings it up again, with the password its data was made with.

What serviceman makes on that machine, through its docker's Engine API, reached over the agent's link:

What Its name What it is for
container serviceman-db-<name> the server, restarted with docker (unless-stopped): a restart of serviceman or of the agent touches nothing of it
volume serviceman-db-<name> its data, at /var/lib/mysql or /var/lib/postgresql/data
network serviceman-databases where an app in a container reaches it, by its container's name
port 127.0.0.1:<port> where a program on that machine reaches it; docker picks the port, and nothing outside the machine reaches it

#A database in it

+ Database makes an empty one, its name up to 32 small letters, digits and _, with a user of its own named after it, whose rights are on that database alone. In PostgreSQL the user owns it, and nobody else may connect to it: PostgreSQL lets every user connect to every database unless told otherwise.

#The passwords

serviceman makes root's password and every user's, and keeps them in data/databases.json, mode 600, beside what it writes about itself: never in the config, never in an answer to the page. They reach the machine in the bodies of the Engine API's requests, the container's environment and an exec's, never on a command line, which every user of the machine can read. The SQL that makes a user goes into the container as a file only root reads, and is removed once it ran.

An app's DATABASE_URL carries its user's password. A program on the machine itself gets it in the environment the agent starts it with. A container gets it as every variable of its env does, on the docker run line on that machine for the moment it runs; the agent's log writes it DATABASE_URL=***.

#Samples

Sample What it is Fetched from Licence
Sakila a DVD rental shop, 47 thousand rows: 16 tables in MySQL, 21 in PostgreSQL jOOQ's sakila on GitHub, commit e089a5b BSD-2-Clause
Chinook a music store, 11 tables, 15 thousand rows lerocha/chinook-database on GitHub, release v1.4.5 MIT

Each engine has its own files of each sample. PostgreSQL's Sakila loads into a database made for it first, afresh; its Chinook makes its own.

Each file is fetched once by serviceman from that address, pinned to that commit or release, kept in data/samples/ under its sha256, and loaded only when its sha256 is the one written in database_samples.js. A file that changed there is refused: the server fails, saying the sha256 it found, and nothing of it is run. The sample's database gets a user of its own, as one made with + Database does.

#An app picks one

In an app's Settings on Apps, its Data tab: + Database lists the databases of every server, those on the app's own machine with a user serviceman made to pick, the others greyed, saying why. The pick is written into the app's config as databases, each one variable of its env:

{
    "name": "adminer",
    "type": "docker",
    "remotes": ["laptop"],
    "image": "adminer",
    "publish": {"host": "adminer.localhost", "port": 8080},
    "databases": [{"server": "mysql-1", "database": "sakila", "env": "DATABASE_URL"}]
}

At every start the variable holds the database's own user, its password and where the app reaches it:

mysql://sakila:<password>@serviceman-db-mysql-1:3306/sakila     an app in a container
mysql://sakila:<password>@127.0.0.1:<port>/sakila                a program on the machine
postgresql://sakila:<password>@serviceman-db-postgresql-1:5432/sakila

An app in a container, a docker image or a program in an image, is put on the serviceman-databases network to reach the server there. A pick of another machine's database, or of one that is not there or not up, stops the start with the reason, rather than start an app that finds no database. The tab shows the URL with its password as dots: the page never has it.

#Adminer

An app of Adminer's own image (adminer, any tag) given a database opens on its DATABASE_URL, logged in as its user, for a visitor signed in through its wall: serviceman puts a plugin into the container as it starts (src/main/adminer/serviceman_database.php). serviceman says who the visitor is in X-Auth-User and drops any a visitor sends, so the plugin lets in only whom the wall let in. Without a wall it lets nobody in and says so; a server typed in its form is never reached. Its Data tab says which of the two it is.

The single adminer.php does the same: dropped on Apps, it runs on the machine picked, in serviceman's PHP image (a PHP file), and its folder holds the plugin and the adminer-plugins.php that Adminer loads beside itself. Its container is made on serviceman-databases, by an agent that can (an older one joins it once it is made).

#Remove

Remove… asks for the server's name typed again, then takes its container and its volume away, with every database in it. An app that picked one of them stops at its next start, saying so. A machine that is offline keeps them: Remove is refused until it is back.

#For whoever runs it

Where What is there
data/databases.json the servers, their root passwords and their users, mode 600
data/samples/<sha256>.sql the samples, as fetched
docker ps --filter label=serviceman.database the servers' containers, on their machine
docker logs serviceman-db-<name> what MySQL or PostgreSQL said, on its machine
database_* in serviceman's log each server brought up, made, removed (The log)
